title: AI action required, as APRA reveals new plans
full_text:
Australia’s banks, insurers, and super funds will be expected to do more on key areas of concern, but the prudential regulator will wind back some controls as part of a push to lighten the load.
Publishing its new plans on Thursday, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority said it was “getting the balance right” on stability of the financial sector, without loading up companies with burdensome rules and controls.
APRA is charged with ensuring the pillars of Australia’s financial sector are safe, sound, and secure.
But some criticise the regulator for being too risk averse.
APRA chair John Lonsdale said it was concerned about the sluggish growth and inflation haunting both the Australian and global economies.
“Geopolitical tensions continue to have economic impacts on inflation, trade relationships and cost-of-living pressures,” he said.
“At the same time, technological developments are creating new threats and amplifying older ones, while also creating competitive challenges for traditional business models.”
Mr Lonsdale said APRA was trying to respond to these challenges by pushing regulated institutions to strengthen their systems around cyber attacks and the potential for AI-powered hacks.
“We will also continue to support productivity, further reducing burden on industry through initiatives that streamline and simplify our prudential standards,” he said.
Among its priorities this year, APRA told regulated companies to expect a continued push on increased cyber resilience.
In April, APRA wrote to banks, insurers, and super funds outlining expectations for dealing with AI-related risks.
APRA is worried companies are too keen to capitalise on the use of AI internally, in an attempt to save money, without considering flow-on impacts or risks.
Mr Lonsdale noted APRA itself was also looking at how it uses AI.
He said this was “to make sure we are ready for future challenges, that we improve our agility and that we strengthen our productivity and impact”.
APRA faces a constrained budget this year, with funding to the agency down by $2m to $278m.
Headcount will also contract from 907 to 900.
In addition, APRA is concerned some companies across the financial sector have all concentrated on common technology platforms or providers, putting at risk the broad financial sector in the event of an outage.
Many companies have piled into particular technologies or hosting services, leaving key parts of the sector exposed.
APRA said it planned to probe Australia’s banks over their lending, in particular loans to small and medium customers.
The recent profit season saw banks point to business lending as a key growth area, amid sluggish housing credit growth.
APRA said this lending had to “remain prudent given the potential for less favourable economic conditions”.
The superannuation sector has also been put on notice, with APRA telling trustees that they will be required to commission independent reviews of governance.
APRA has repeatedly clashed with the super sector, attempting to force funds to flick long-time directors last year.
But Mr Lonsdale said APRA was also looking at “a range of initiatives that are delivering meaningful cost savings for industry”.
Australia’s financial sector has long lobbied for a roll-back of some controls and regulations, warning they doubled up with other regulators or loaded up institutions with costs for little benefit to the end consumer.
